nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; nonsense verse, the limerick and the landscape traveller
literary_identity: Poet, painter and illustrator; the inventor of the modern nonsense poem and the greatest English writer for children after Carroll.
biography: Born in Highgate, London, on 12 May 1812, the twentieth child of a stockbroker; he was raised by his elder sister Ann and earned his living from the age of fifteen as an ornithological draughtsman, drawing the parrots for the Zoological Society. He published A Book of Nonsense in 1846 for the grandchildren of his patron the Earl of Derby, and spent the rest of his life travelling in Italy, Greece, Egypt and India, publishing illustrated journals of his journeys. He suffered from epilepsy and from loneliness all his life and died at San Remo on 29 January 1888.
literary_profile: Lear invented the modern nonsense poem: his limericks, his 'Nonsense Botany' and 'Nonsense Alphabets', and above all The Owl and the Pussy-cat and The Jumblies, create a world of pure verbal play in which melancholy and absurdity are inseparable. He was also a superb landscape painter and travel writer, and his nonsense is the other side of Victorian earnestness — a private, melancholy man making a world of impossible creatures who are nonetheless entirely at home in it.
stylistic_characteristics: Closed stanzaic forms pushed to absurdity; invented words and impossible creatures; the perfect rhythmic and rhyming control of nonsense; the comic drawing integrated with the text; the melancholy undertow beneath the play; the topographical journal with comic illustrations.
intellectual_concerns: Nonsense, play and the liberation of language; travel, exile and the loneliness of the wanderer; childhood and the freedom of the imagination; the absurdity of social forms; landscape and the picturesque; melancholy and the consolations of art.
historical_significance: Lear is the founder of the modern nonsense tradition and one of the most beloved poets in English: his limericks established a form, The Owl and the Pussy-cat and The Jumblies are among the most quoted poems in the language, and his nonsense gave twentieth-century poetry and children's literature their model of verbal freedom.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the classical lyric and the poetry of the Shropshire lad
literary_identity: Poet and classical scholar; the author of A Shropshire Lad, the most popular sequence of English lyrics of the 1890s.
biography: Born Alfred Edward Housman at Fockbury, Worcestershire, on 26 March 1859, the son of a solicitor; his mother died when he was twelve, and he failed his final examinations at Oxford in 1881, an experience he never explained. He worked as a patent clerk in London for ten years while writing the poems of A Shropshire Lad (1896), became Professor of Latin at University College London in 1892 and at Cambridge in 1911, and was the greatest textual critic of his age. He published only one other volume, Last Poems (1922), and died at Cambridge on 30 April 1936.
literary_profile: Housman wrote the English lyric at its most concentrated: his poems of the Shropshire countryside, of young men dying, of love that cannot be spoken and of the indifference of the universe are among the most technically perfect in the language. He was also a scholar of immense severity, and the tension between the dry classical editor and the passionate lyric poet is the central fact of his work — his poems are short, plain, and utterly without consolation.
stylistic_characteristics: The ballad and the song measure in quatrains; plain diction and short lines; the refrain and the refrain-like repetition; bitter irony and understatement; the rural English landscape as a stage for mortality; the deliberate withholding of feeling.
intellectual_concerns: Early death, youth and the brevity of life; unspoken and unlawful love; the indifference of nature and of the universe; the English countryside and the passage of the seasons; the soldier, the criminal and the exile; stoicism as the only available response.
historical_significance: Housman is the most widely read English poet of his generation after Kipling: A Shropshire Lad became a talisman for the generation of 1914, its poems were set by Vaughan Williams, Butterworth and Gurney, and its example shaped English lyric poetry from Hardy to Larkin. He is also the finest English poet of suppressed and unavowable desire.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Scottish; the children's fantasy and the sentimental Scottish comedy
literary_identity: Dramatist and novelist; the creator of Peter Pan and the most popular Scottish writer of the age.
biography: Born James Matthew Barrie at Kirriemuir, Angus, on 9 May 1860, the ninth child of a hand-loom weaver; he was educated at Edinburgh University and worked as a journalist in Nottingham and London before his Scottish sketches, collected as Auld Licht Idylls (1888) and A Window in Thrums (1889), made him famous. His novels The Little Minister (1891) and Sentimental Tommy (1896) were best-sellers; he turned to the stage in 1897, and Peter Pan was first performed in 1904. He was made a baronet in 1913 and died in London on 19 June 1937.
literary_profile: Barrie wrote the English and Scottish sentimental comedy and the fantasy of childhood: his Peter Pan is the central myth of the modern imagination of childhood — the boy who will not grow up, the island of lost boys, the fairy and the pirate — and his plays and Scottish sketches are full of a delicate, ironic tenderness for small lives and lost mothers. His work is also one of the great Victorian and Edwardian studies of grief: the death of his brother David, on whom he modelled Peter, haunted everything he wrote.
stylistic_characteristics: Kailyard comedy of Scottish village life with exact dialect; whimsy and pathos held together by irony; stage directions of extraordinary detail; the child's point of view rendered without condescension; the fantasy that is also a study of loss.
intellectual_concerns: Childhood and the refusal to grow up; motherhood and the loss of the mother; Scotland, the village and the kailyard; fantasy and escape; time and memory; money, class and the small town.
historical_significance: Barrie is the most popular Scottish writer of his age and the creator of Peter Pan, the most influential children's myth of the twentieth century: the play gave the language a permanent figure, its royalties endowed Great Ormond Street Hospital, and its treatment of childhood and grief has made it a central text of modern children's literature and of Scottish writing.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the comic travel book and the farce
literary_identity: Humorist, novelist and playwright; the author of Three Men in a Boat, the most durable English comic book of the century.
biography: Born Jerome Klapka Jerome at Walsall, Staffordshire, on 2 May 1859, the son of a coal-mine owner and lay preacher who died in poverty; he left school at fourteen and worked as a railway clerk, a schoolmaster, a journalist and an actor before Three Men in a Boat (1889) made him famous. He founded and edited The Idler (1892-97) and wrote many plays and essays; he died at Northampton on 14 June 1927.
literary_profile: Jerome wrote the modern comic travel book: Three Men in a Boat takes the Victorian vogue for the Thames excursion and turns it into a shaggy-dog narrative of three incompetent young men, a dog and a great deal of unnecessary luggage, in which the comedy lies in the gap between the heroic intention and the domestic disaster. He was also a considerable comic playwright and a gentle satirist of the late-Victorian office and suburb.
stylistic_characteristics: Digressive, anecdotal first-person narration; the comic list and the escalating catalogue; deadpan reporting of absurdity; the mock-heroic treatment of trivial mishaps; self-deprecating irony; dialogue of three friends who talk past one another.
intellectual_concerns: Holiday, leisure and the English weekend; friendship and masculine companionship; the comic body, illness and medicine; the suburb and the office; the Thames and the English landscape; the gap between pretension and performance.
historical_significance: Jerome is the funniest English writer of the 1890s and Three Men in a Boat one of the small number of English comic classics: it has never been out of print, it made the comic travel book a genre, and its tone — self-mocking, humane, digressive — is the model for English comic writing from Wodehouse to Bryson.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the naturalist novel, the war report and the ironist of the city
literary_identity: Novelist, poet and war correspondent; the author of The Red Badge of Courage and the founder of American literary naturalism.
biography: Born in Newark, New Jersey, on 1 November 1871, the fourteenth child of a Methodist minister; he was educated at Lafayette College and Syracuse University without taking a degree, and worked as a journalist in New York, where he wrote Maggie: A Girl of the Streets (1893) at his own expense. The Red Badge of Courage (1895) made him internationally famous; he went to the war in Cuba in 1896-97, was shipwrecked on the Commodore, and died of tuberculosis at Badenweiler, Germany, on 5 June 1900, aged twenty-eight.
literary_profile: Crane invented American naturalism: Maggie and The Red Badge of Courage take the poor of the Bowery and the soldier in battle and record them without moralising, in a prose of brilliant colour and cold distance. He was also the first great American war correspondent, and his best stories — 'The Open Boat', 'The Blue Hotel' — are among the finest in the language: his irony, his imagery and his refusal of consolation changed what American fiction could do.
stylistic_characteristics: Impressionist colour and vivid sensory notation; the ironic narrator who withholds judgement; the short sentence and the stark scene; dialogue in dialect from the street; the refusal of a moral or a comforting ending; the image that becomes the story's meaning.
intellectual_concerns: Poverty, drink and the urban poor; war, fear and the illusions of courage; the indifference of nature; the city and the slum; the individual against a determining environment; the failure of the American promise.
historical_significance: Crane is the father of American naturalism and the most influential American prose stylist of the 1890s: The Red Badge of Courage changed the literature of war, 'The Open Boat' is one of the great American stories, and his example made possible Norris, London, Dreiser and Hemingway.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the naturalist epic and the romance of the West
literary_identity: Novelist and journalist; the author of McTeague and The Octopus and the leading American theorist of naturalism.
biography: Born Benjamin Franklin Norris in Chicago on 5 March 1870; the family moved to San Francisco in 1884 and he studied art in Paris, then English at Berkeley and Harvard. He worked as a war correspondent in South Africa and Cuba, joined the San Francisco Wave and McClure's, and published McTeague in 1899 and The Octopus in 1901. He died of peritonitis in San Francisco on 25 October 1902, aged thirty-two, leaving the unfinished epic of which The Pit was the second volume.
literary_profile: Norris wrote the American naturalist epic: his subject is the great determining forces — greed, wheat, the railroad, the brute inheritance — and his method is the 'romance of the real', in which the individual is destroyed by powers larger than himself. The Octopus is the central American novel of the railroad and the wheat country, and McTeague is the first great American novel of the urban poor: his theoretical essays on naturalism defined the movement for his generation.
stylistic_characteristics: Large-scale epic structure with interlacing stories; the documentary description of an industry; the recurring symbolic motif (the wheat, the tooth, the railroad); the sudden eruption of violence; the scientific and biological analysis of character; a romantic rhetoric at odds with naturalist doctrine.
intellectual_concerns: The railroad, the wheat and the agrarian revolt; greed, money and the ownership of land; the brute inheritance and the animal in man; the West and the city; the class war of the 1890s; the American empire in Cuba and the Philippines.
historical_significance: Norris is the theorist and the epic novelist of American naturalism: The Octopus is the greatest American novel of the railroad and one of the central documents of the populist revolt, McTeague founded the American novel of the urban poor, and his essays defined the movement that carried American fiction into the twentieth century.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the adventure romance, the socialist tract and the novel of the North
literary_identity: Novelist, journalist and socialist; the most widely read American writer of his time and the author of The Call of the Wild.
biography: Born John Griffith Chaney in San Francisco on 12 January 1876, the illegitimate son of an astrologer and a spiritualist; he left school at thirteen and worked in a cannery, as an oyster pirate, a sailor and a tramp, and was jailed for vagrancy in 1894. He joined the Klondike gold rush in 1897 and began writing on his return; The Call of the Wild (1903) and The Sea-Wolf (1904) made him rich. He joined the Socialist Party, wrote The Iron Heel and Martin Eden, and died at Glen Ellen, California, on 22 November 1916.
literary_profile: London wrote the American adventure story as a vehicle of ideas: his Klondike tales are stories of survival at the limit of nature, and his novels carry a socialist and Darwinian argument about the struggle for existence and the class war. He was also the first American writer to make a fortune from the mass magazine market, and his best work — The Call of the Wild, 'To Build a Fire', Martin Eden — is unmatched in the American literature of the far north.
stylistic_characteristics: Direct, vigorous narrative in the first person or close third; the ordeal narrative of survival; the animal's point of view; the documentary account of work at sea, in the mines and on the trail; the socialist argument carried by plot; the return to the primitive.
intellectual_concerns: Survival, the struggle for existence and the call of the wild; the Klondike and the frontier north; socialism and the class war; the sea and the working sailor; the artist and the market; the primitive and the civilised.
historical_significance: London is the most widely translated American writer of his era and a central figure in the American literature of naturalism and of socialism: The Call of the Wild has never been out of print, 'To Build a Fire' is the classic American story of the wilderness, and his Klondike fiction created the modern myth of the north.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the novel of manners, the social satire and the ghost story
literary_identity: Novelist, short-story writer and designer; the first woman to win the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction and the finest American novelist of manners.
biography: Born Edith Newbold Jones in New York on 24 January 1862 into a family of the old Knickerbocker aristocracy; she was educated privately and in Europe, married Edward Wharton in 1885, and published The Decoration of Houses with Ogden Codman in 1897. The House of Mirth (1905) made her famous; she lived in Paris from 1907, divorced in 1913, and was decorated for her relief work in the First World War. She won the Pulitzer Prize in 1921 for The Age of Innocence and died at Saint-Brice-sous-Forêt, France, on 11 August 1937.
literary_profile: Wharton wrote the American novel of manners with a European severity: her subject is the New York aristocracy and the individual trapped by its codes, and her method is the ironic, beautifully built narrative in which the social surface is described with absolute precision and the moral cost is allowed to emerge without comment. She was also a superb writer of ghost stories and a serious critic of American culture, and no one has written better about the small cruelty of a society that has no visible power except opinion.
stylistic_characteristics: Precise, ironic exposition of a social world; the withheld judgement; symbolic architecture and interiors; the tragic or near-tragic ending that the social code makes inevitable; dialogue that carries the pressure of what cannot be said; the elegant chapter ending.
intellectual_concerns: The New York aristocracy and its codes; marriage, divorce and the marriage market; money and the new rich against the old; the American and Europe; the woman of intelligence in a society that has no use for it; the ghost and the supernatural.
historical_significance: Wharton is the finest American novelist of manners and the first woman to win the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction: The Age of Innocence, The House of Mirth and The Custom of the Country are permanent classics, her ghost stories are among the best in the language, and her portrait of old New York is the essential record of the American upper class.
